title: Pipe replacement at national-leading pace
headline: 401 km of water and sewer pipes replaced (2022–2025)
plain_language: Ageing pipes burst and leak. Replacing them means fewer sewage spills, fewer water losses, and more reliable taps — especially in townships where dignity starts with working sanitation.
why_it_matters: Between 2022 and 2025 Cape Town replaced three times more water and sewer pipes than Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni combined — a delivery fact the Mayor can stand on.

evidence.label: Peer comparison
evidence.value: 3× more pipe km than JHB + Tshwane + Ekurhuleni combined

next_step: Keep the R2bn pipe-replacement line ring-fenced through mid-year review.

title: City of Hope infrastructure programme protected
headline: R40bn three-year basic infrastructure investment adopted
plain_language: This is the City’s long-term build programme for water, power, roads and transport — the bones of a working metro. Protecting it means Capetonians keep getting services that other metros are losing.
why_it_matters: Council adopted the 2026/27 City of Hope budget with the full R40bn infrastructure run-rate intact, while expanding rates relief.
image_credit: Unsplash — Cape Town / Table Mountain vista (illustrative)

evidence.label: Coverage
evidence.value: ~75% of infrastructure spend benefits lower-income households (City claim)

next_step: Publish a public capital delivery tracker by ward for the R40bn programme.

title: Widest rates relief among SA metros
headline: Rates-free threshold raised R450k → R620k
plain_language: Property rates are the monthly tax on a home’s value. Raising the rates-free threshold means more lower- and middle-value homes pay nothing (or less) in rates — putting money back into household budgets.
why_it_matters: Creates political space and resident goodwill while the City still funds a record capital programme.

evidence.label: City claim
evidence.value: Widest rates relief / competitive monthly bills vs SA metros

next_step: Pair the relief message with a clear ‘what your rates fund’ ward brief.

title: Record safety budget and LEAP capacity growth
headline: R6.8bn safety & security · policing personnel +50% this term
plain_language: LEAP (Law Enforcement Advancement Plan) puts additional officers into high-crime precincts. A larger, better-funded safety budget means more visible patrols where murders and contact crime concentrate.
why_it_matters: Safety is the top resident anxiety. The City has grown policing capacity by more than 50% over four years (+1,340 officers) and tabled a record safety budget.

evidence.label: LEAP areas (Q3 2025/26)
evidence.value: Murder rate −3.7% in combined LEAP precincts (external analysis — confirm SAPS quarter)

next_step: Attach the exact SAPS quarter and precinct list before any crime claim in the room.

title: MyCiTi Cape Flats expansion funded
headline: R3.2–R3.3bn toward Mitchells Plain / Khayelitsha expansion
plain_language: MyCiTi is the City’s bus rapid transit system. Expanding it into the Cape Flats means shorter, safer, more reliable trips for residents who depend on public transport — not private cars.
why_it_matters: Described by the City as the largest investment of its kind in South Africa; connects opportunity to historically underserved areas.

evidence.label: Priority corridors
evidence.value: Mitchells Plain and Khayelitsha expansion called out in Mayor’s speech

next_step: Publish monthly ridership and construction milestones for the Cape Flats corridors.

title: Public lighting outages trending down
headline: Faults falling ~2.7% per period — safer streets at night
plain_language: When streetlights fail, streets feel less safe and crime risk rises after dark. A falling outage trend means maintenance is catching up — lights stay on where people walk and wait for transport.
why_it_matters: One of the few operational metrics currently improving in the Helm twin — a tangible ‘basics better’ win.
next_step: Map remaining dark spots by ward and publish a 90-day fix list.
